categories.title: TROPHIES
categories.blurb: How scores, stars and aging work.

blocks.p: A trophy's score is all its measurements' points added up.
Each species has four score lines. They are on every animal's page (Animals tab, under Trophy):
Females of whitetail, mule deer, moose, elk, bison, kudu and pronghorn have no score lines, so they get no trophy stars. Every harvest still gets a separate hunt rating for the shot.

list: The lines are the same for males and females. What differs is how big each sex can grow.
Stars are set when the trophy is measured. The hunting log keeps them only for animals you harvest.

articles.title: How measurements become points
articles.subtitle: Whole numbers times points per unit

blocks.p: points = measurement (decimals dropped) x points per unit

blocks.note: Example: a 0.86 kg yellow-billed duck hen = 860 g / 5 = 172 points = 2 stars.

list: Lengths are in centimeters and the decimals are cut off, not rounded: 63.9 cm counts as 63.
Racks, horns, tusks and body length score 1 point per cm. Skull length and width score 10 points per cm.

Weight trophies: points = weight in grams / grams per point. 5 g: mallard, yellow-billed duck, snowshoe hare. 2 g: ptarmigan. 50 g: turkey, honey badger. 100 g: wolverine. Zebra scores 1 point per kg and ostrich 2 points per kg.
Whitetail: both 'length of typical points' and 'length of all points' count. Non-typical points don't grow in the game yet, so the two are the same and every tine counts twice.
Elk: 'length of all points' only counts on the rare racks with extra points. It's worth hundreds of points, so those racks jump a star or two.
Mule deer: only typical points are measured.

blocks.p: Age and fitness together give a growth value between 0 and 1:

blocks.note: growth = (age x fitness - offset) / (oldest age - offset), kept between 0 and 1. Fitness counts as a fraction here (83% = 0.83). offset = a tenth of the species' starting age (0.1 for animals that start at 1 year).

list: An animal's fitness is set when it is born and never changes; only its age goes up.
Growth 1.0 is the maximum size. It needs age x fitness = oldest age, so only an animal at the oldest age with 100% fitness gets there.
Half the age or half the fitness is roughly half the size.
Body size, weight, skulls and body length follow growth in a straight line: value = minimum + (maximum - minimum) x growth.
Skull, body-length and weight trophies use growth at the moment of the kill.
Antlers, horns and tusks are rebuilt every year from the animal's new age (see How racks are built and how they age).

articles.title: Skulls, weights and racks
articles.subtitle: Which trophies are luck and which aren't

blocks.p: No luck: the same age and fitness always give the same score. Skulls (wolf, grizzly, lion, spotted hyena) score (length + width) x 10.
Crocodile body length: bulls 170-640 cm, cows 150-450 cm.

list: Type: every species has one rack type per sex (moose bulls are the exception, see Moose below).
Warthog sows grow tusks too, the same kind as the boars.
Size: every beam, tine and horn section grows with age x fitness, up to its maximum.
Shape: the bends are rolled at random for each side, so two animals with the same age and fitness can score differently - and the roll is redone every year.

Tines: an age table gives the trophy a level from 0 to 6 that decides which tines may grow; many tines also need a minimum age and fitness. Whitetail buck: age 1 = level 0, 2 = 1, 3 = 2, 4 = 3, 5 = 4, 6 = 5, 7 and older = 6.
Measuring: straight lines between the joints of the finished trophy, turned into points.

A moose bull has one of four antler types: cervina, semi-cervina, half palm or full palm. It is picked by his fitness when his first rack is built and kept for life: cervina 0-20%, semi-cervina 10-30%, half palm 30-100%, full palm 40-100%. Where the bands overlap the pick is random.
Each type has its own age table. Cervina and semi-cervina have no palm, so their palm width is 0.
Main beam: the longest straight line from the antler base to the tip of the palm (or the last tine), on the left antler.
Palm width: the widest point of each palm, left plus right. It grows with the antler thickness value, so it follows age x fitness.
Outside spread: the widest distance between matching tines on the left and right antler. It comes from the random bends, so it changes every year.
Number of points: every tine that shows, both sides counted.
Moose tines that do not grow are folded back into the palm, so missing tines also change the palm's shape.
A rack is made the first time the animal spawns near you.
Every in-game year the animal gets a year older and its rack is made again from scratch.

Which tines grow depends on age and fitness. A few are a coin flip.
The bends, and with them the spreads, are random and change every year.
Left and right are rolled separately.

categories.title: HERDS
categories.blurb: Herd fitness, herd size, culling and habitat enhancements.

blocks.p: Each animal has its own herd fitness on every land, from 0 to 100%. The game shows it as the herd's state:
A herd right on a line (30%, 60%, 90%) counts as the lower state.

blocks.note: These are the herd's numbers, not single animals. Animals are born around the herd's fitness and can be up to 50% fitter than it, so a Stable herd at 50% can still hold a 90% animal (see How herd fitness reaches the animals).

list: A herd starts at a random fitness inside its land's start range (on each animal's page).
A herd never drops below 20%.
A herd never rises above its cap. Base caps are 50%, 60%, 70% or 80%, so no herd can be Thriving on its base cap.
Each habitat enhancement built for an animal on a land raises that cap by +10%, up to 100%. Thriving needs enhancements.

articles.title: What a harvest does to the herd
articles.subtitle: Culling

blocks.p: Every harvest changes the herd's fitness right away. The game compares the animal with the herd: difference = herd fitness - animal's fitness.

list: Animal less fit than the herd: herd fitness goes up.
Animal fitter than the herd: herd fitness goes down.
Same fitness: no change.

blocks.note: change = gap value x sex x age x upward bonus

list: Sex: males x1.0; females x1.2 for most animals (x1.15 moose; x1.1 warthog, buffalo, hare; x1.05 wolf, grizzly, ducks, ptarmigan).
Age: young animals count most - x1.3 at the youngest, x1.25 at 30 % of the oldest age, x1.05 at 70 %, x1.0 at the oldest.
Upward bonus, only when the herd goes up: x1.3 for whitetail, mule deer, elk, pronghorn, Dall sheep, zebra, ostrich, turkey and buffalo; x1.15 for the rest.
The result is held between 20% and the cap.
Elk herd at 60%, take a young cow at 30%: 3.25% x 1.2 x ~1.27 x 1.3 = about +6.4%.
Same herd, take a prime old bull at 90%: 3.25% x 1.0 x ~1.03 = about -3.3%.

blocks.p: Cull the weak, the young and the females to raise a herd. Every top animal you shoot pulls it down a little.

articles.title: How herd fitness reaches the animals
articles.subtitle: The fitness roll for new animals

blocks.p: New animals that join a herd get their fitness rolled around the herd's fitness:

list: a bell curve centered on the herd fitness, with a spread of 25%,
kept within 50% of the herd fitness, never below 10% and never above 100%.

blocks.p: A herd at 80% mostly produces animals between 55% and 100%, so the rare 95-100 % animals come from high-fitness herds. A herd at 40% almost never makes one. Fitter animals grow bigger trophies (and only moose bulls at 40% or more can grow a full palm).

articles.title: Herd size
articles.subtitle: How many animals a herd has, and why

blocks.p: Every herd lives in its own territory, and every territory is one of four types: Big, Medium, Small or Solitary. Each animal has its own numbers for each type (below). A herd's type never changes.

blocks.h: How herd fitness changes the size

list: When a map is first made, every herd gets a random number of animals inside its range.

Every game year, right after the animals age, the game counts each herd. A herd with fewer animals than its number for this year gets young animals until it has that many. Their fitness is rolled around the herd's fitness.

The number for the year comes from the herd fitness: the lowest starting fitness of that animal on that land gives the smallest herd, the top gives the biggest. The top is 100% on private lands and the land's base cap on public lands.
A herd never loses animals this way. Only hunting and old age make it smaller, so an overhunted herd stays small until the next year.

blocks.note: number = smallest + (biggest - smallest + 1) x how far the herd fitness is between the land's lowest start and the top, rounded down, and never above the biggest

list: Big elk herd (11-18) on a private land where elk start from 31%:
herd fitness 31% (Stable): 11 elk, 45%: 12, 60%: 14, 75% (Healthy): 16, 90%: 17, 100% (Thriving): 18.

blocks.p: So a Vulnerable herd grows back to few animals, a Thriving one to its biggest. Raise the herd fitness (cull the weak, build habitat enhancements on private land) and every herd of that animal on the land grows back bigger next year. The herd card on the map shows each herd's type, how many animals it has now and its number for next year.

The binocular settings were mixed up: 'Binoculars mode' is Hold or Toggle.

blocks.p: Spot-and-stalk suits animals that prefer open terrain, such as mule deer.
Once you have a good view, look through your binoculars to spot animals. Eventually, you'll see them—or at least hear them.

One common rookie blunder is moving right in. Instead, check the wind direction below your compass, then scan for natural cover and landmarks. Is there a longer but safer approach to the shooting spot?
If you're unsure how much noise you make and how visible you are, look at the indicators on the bottom-left of your screen. These aren't superprecise, but they give you decent estimates.
Once you approach the shooting spot, the animal may not be positioned well for a clean shot. So it's never a bad idea to have the right caller on you.

The smartest bucks are notoriously skittish. Often the only way to get ahead is to predict their route, hide in thick foliage and wait patiently. Rookies find it boring, but it's effective—as long as you remain virtually non-existent.
Not enough natural cover? Or you just can't see a damn thing? Blinds and stands are at your service. Open blinds offer better visibility and shooting angles, closed ones provide better cover.
Even when you plan meticulously, animals will still find ways to avoid you, almost as if they have a sixth sense! So consider using a luring scent when they are passing by.

After you release a scent, it's carried downwind. It won't last for longer than a minute, so release it again in time. Give it enough tries: the animal will catch it and will start approaching your position.

At this point, you should conceal yourself in a blind or a stand. Otherwise, the animal may catch your scent. When you're far away from the target, call it with a caller first and only release the scent once the animal is closer to get it just where you want it.
Still-hunting is especially useful for small animals that love dense cover (but not only for them!).
The key is to move slowly—VERY slowly—and stop frequently to observe and listen. Eventually, you should spot a hare hiding in thickets without spooking it.
This is your opening! Once you spot it, your shot window may be very short-lived. Make it clean, but don't waste too much time, or you'll spook your target.

Unlike fully terrestrial game large and small, waterfowl and landfowl birds are hunted with shotguns equipped with shell ammunition. Hunting them is a different art that may require both stalking and ambushing.

Decoys may appear fake to you, but to birds they're convincing enough. Place them around the area where birds congregate (the more, the merrier!), hide in a nearby blind, then wait for the target to notice one of them and approach it.
When it happens, the bird may still not be close enough for a good shot, so that's when you call it. Given the right pauses between calls, it'll eventually come close enough. Now, it's time to flush!

Traditionally, hunters take birds on the wing, meaning they flush them into flight before shooting. Some consider this the only ethical way, but most hunters agree that as long as you use the appropriate ammunition and strive for clean shots, you can't go wrong.

Waterfowls are erratic and don't really commit to a single area the way landfowl do. They fly around so much that many hunters prefer to just shoot them when they happen to be passing overhead. Again, as long as you go for a clean shot, you're doing good.

When certain techniques just don't click, activate their Skills. Earn Skill Points used for Skills by harvesting animals and completing Challenges. Each Skill corresponds to a playstyle; you can't activate them all, so pick the ones that will help you with something you're struggling with!
Driving can get you around really quickly. But it also spooks all nearby animals, so only bring your vehicle when you're exploring.
As you explore, place tents in the remote locations you expect to revisit. Eventually, you'll have a Map full of accessible travel points!
When you find something worth revisiting, don't hesitate to leave a Marker. You can place Markers both on your Map and in the environment.

As you explore Reserves, you'll inevitably discover a lot of animal Tracks. When you want to obtain more information, get closer to analyze them. But you only need to walk near them to have them marked on your Map.
Be daring, but don't be dumb! Some risks aren't worth taking: you might lose consciousness, and wake up back in your Lodge, potentially far away from wherever you were exploring.
Taking care of animals means taking care of their habitat. Animals won't grow up healthy if they drink poor quality water and don't have enough food.

See where the animals are living for yourself. Gradually visit stations on public land and private cabins to learn where the landmarks are and open up your Map. Pay special attention to Campsites, as this is where you'll find Mission assignments.

Conditions will never be perfect in the publicly maintained lands. However, they at least adhere to certain standards, while private properties depend on their owner. While some are in decent shape, others are in dire need of proper maintenance.

On certain private property, you'll find sources of land and water pollution. These harm every animal that lives in the vicinity. Unless you fix the problem, these animals will never live up to their potential!
Find every source of pollution, approach and fix it. It might cost a fortune, but animals in the area will grow up fitter than ever!
Don't rely on luck! Unless you hunt prepared, the best animals will outsmart you in the wild.
Learn about the animal Species you target in your Encyclopedia. As you analyze animals and their Tracks, you gain more information on each Species.

Identify the biomes animals prefer: certain species may prefer or avoid dense forests, open fields, mountains, and so on. Second, see what their lifestyle is, as some move around a lot while others stay in more or less the same area.

See what strengths and weaknesses the animal species has. Animals usually rely on certain senses and neglect others. For example, animals with a good sense of smell often have poor eyesight. Exploit these weaknesses!

Open your Map and look for where the animal lives. If you aren't sure what the landscape is like, go and check it out in person! While you're at it, scout the best vantage points and well-covered spots. Leave a Marker there so you don't forget.

There isn't only a place for everything, but also a time. Your Map shows when animals drink, eat and rest. Their internal clocks are precise, but they still have to travel from one spot to another, so don't expect them to always be on time.

Hearth & Hunt's weather forecasts are famously accurate. Check them on your Map so that rain and thunderstorms don't ruin your hunts. If you don't want to wait, consider resting at your Lodge, Cabins or tents—time will pass in a moment.
Consider your Backpack before hunting. With a smaller one, you'll make less noise. If you don't have a backpack, you'll be even more silent.

At first, you won't have that much Gear to bring on your hunts. As you gradually unlock and buy more Gear at the Shop, make use of all the space in your current Backpack, as additional Gear won't produce more noise as long as your Backpack stays the same.

You'll only get one shot. To learn to get it right, there's no better place than the Shooting range near your Lodge. You can practice on targets with the vital organs marked, indicating where to shoot.

Before setting off, consider taking on one of the Mission assignments from Campsites. They can get quite challenging, so make sure you equip the appropriate long-range scope, or optics with night or thermal vision if you plan to hunt outside the conventional hours.

Firearms without attachments are like bucks with shed racks. The base is there, but it feels incomplete. In most cases, you at least need a sight, and there are other tools to enhance your hunting and help you properly harvest animals.

Picking the right sight is essential. When you shoot from close ranges, pick scopes with low magnification and small lenses. When you prepare for long-range hunting, pick scopes with high magnification and larger lenses. And collimators are great for quickly targeting fast-moving small game and birds.

Night/thermal-vision scopes and clip-ons (attached to the base sight) are essential for hunts in low light. And don't forget about suppressors, as they don't just lower shot noise, they also reduce recoil.

Chokes make pellet spreads denser or wider. As of now, you can buy a tight choke to shoot with a denser pattern even from a longer range. One good example is targeting heads or necks of Wild turkeys. But when you target fast-moving small game and birds, you'd rather use the choke installed on the shotgun by default.

Crossbows and bows also have sights, and crossbows support clip-ons. As with rifle scopes, the concept of focal plane comes into play. With first focal plane, the reticle gets larger as you zoom in, making it ideal for long-range shots. With second focal plane, the reticle size doesn't change with more zoom, making it suitable for closer ranges.

Successful and ethical hunting requires appropriate Ammunition. You don't have to be a ballistics nerd though! Open the Encyclopedia to learn the Tier number of the animal Species you're targeting and equip your Weapon with the Ammunition that has that Tier covered.

As you're aiming at an animal, Hunter assist shows you the projected energy of your shot. When it's too low, get closer to the animal. When it's too high, move away. Once you're in the right range, you deal less damage to meat and earn a better Hunt Rating.

You can’t always move. Sometimes, you'll expose yourself or the animal will get away. That's when changing Ammunition from the Radial Inventory comes in. Every Weapon supports Ammunition from only one caliber.

There's enough variation within most Tiers and calibers to prepare yourself for any situation, so don't leave slots in your Ammunition pouch empty. Some Ammunition is free, others you have to buy, and when you run out of it, you'll have to buy more. But as long as it's available in your Storage, it'll be automatically refilled once you open the Inventory.

Which Ammunition of the same Tier should you use in what situations? Look at their penetration and cavity size. Projectiles with higher penetration get even through thick bones. Use them when your shot angle is suboptimal. Projectiles with larger cavities make animals more likely to drop instantly. When your shot angle is great, it'll give you some leeway, as even if you fail to place the shot perfectly, it can still damage their vitals thanks to creating a larger wound.

At first, it often looks as if there are no animals around. This isn't the case! Animals are there, they just know you're coming, and are actively hiding. So how do you find them? You go out and explore!

Look for a high vantage point and scout the area from there with your binoculars. Look carefully, some animals are tough to spot in dense vegetation! If you still can't see them, try looking for animals drinking by larger lakes and rivers, or analyze any Tracks they may have left.

Just like criminals, animals do their best to hide. But they always commit two fatal mistakes: they leave evidence behind (or as we hunters call them, "Tracks"), and they return to the scene of their "crimes" (or activities, such as drinking, feeding, and resting).

If you listen carefully you'll hear audible cues that animals regularly emit. When you analyze the cue, you'll learn which Species it is, the direction where the animal is, and even the approximate distance.

Animals leave footprints and droppings behind. If you spot them while they're still fresh, you can figure out the direction the animal was facing and follow its route: you may eventually get lucky. It's still worth pursuing older Tracks, as they may lead you to permanent ones.

Animal behavior is like clockwork. Animals constantly return to the same Spots to drink, feed, hunt and rest. When you see animals doing one of these activities somewhere, you're likely to see them there the next day as well.

Unless you start to spook them. Once it happens, animals may reconsider if they want to go to the same Spot and start to frequent another one. Thankfully, the overall number of Spots is always limited, so eventually animals will cycle through them all and start going to the original one again.

Now, finding Tracks isn't easy, especially in dense environments. This is where your dog companion comes in. Just give it the command and pay attention. If you want to look for Tracks without your dog, consult the animal articles in your Encyclopedia.

You may get lucky, spotting and approaching animals right away, but when you want to target a specific animal, the most reliable method is to arrive at a likely spot in advance, wait for your target to turn up, and then make your move.

Start by looking for permanent Tracks of animals. When you find them, they are automatically marked on your Map. When animals drink, feed and rest at multiple places, you will see an indication where they are more likely to appear.

Your Map also shows when the animal Species is drinking, feeding, and resting. Just make sure you arrive at the location beforehand so that you have time to hide and don't spook the animals by accident.

The toughest part is waiting. Many hunters don't have the patience and falter at this last step. But if you've planned everything correctly, eventually you'll see the animal arrive, and then it's up to you to take your best shot.

When you make an approach, your goal is to get to the shooting spot without spooking the animal. Before the approach, study the terrain with binoculars to confirm where the animal is and figure out the best path to take.

A good path should provide as much foliage cover as possible, follow a different direction from the way the wind is blowing, and be as short as possible to rule out unpredictable complications. However, if the longer path is safer, it's often the better option.
A good destination has the same qualities as a good path, but it should also be an appropriate shooting spot, with a clear view that enables you to execute a clean shot.

Don't be disappointed when you scan a herd and see only young animals with low Fitness levels. Look closer, as the older animals are smarter and may be hiding in thicker bushes. These leaders of the group are usually the ones with the best Fitness levels and Trophies.
It's often unwise to approach right away. For example, if the animal is on the move, stalk it until it reaches its destination. That's when you make your approach!
Remember that if you spook at least one animal from its herd, the whole group will be spooked soon after.

Only move slowly or VERY slowly. After all, it only takes one loud noise to spook a whole herd. In addition, take short breaks in the spots with more cover. It's always better to test your patience for an extra minute than undermine the whole approach.
Another consideration is your stance. When you're prone, you're better hidden, but you also see less of your surroundings. So crouch when you're on the move, and go prone when you take a break.

As you're approaching, the animal may suddenly start looking in your direction, seem agitated, or even utter a warning sound. Get into cover, stop moving and wait. If you're lucky, it will eventually calm down, then you can proceed.

The visibility indicator suggests how hidden you are. Don't rely solely on it, as even at low visibility, animals can still notice you. If you continue to fail your approaches, dial down the Game Difficulty in the Settings and practice before turning it back up.
The climax of your hunt has come! You're almost ready to draw your weapon and shoot. But before and immediately after that, there's still work to be done.

Before shooting, confirm your target through binoculars. If necessary, mark the animal. It will not only mark the animal itself, but its whole group, on your Map, which will be useful if you botch your shot.
When you draw your weapon and get ready to shoot, use ballistic assists to make sure you don't miss. Also, never shoot without holding your breath!

One of the most important ballistic concepts is the current range (zeroing) of your weapon. As projectiles are subject to gravity, you have to aim higher for long-distance shots. Adjust the range as close to the distance to your target as possible.

Always aim for either the heart or lungs. This way, you ensure both a relatively quick and ethical harvest, as well as higher meat quality. There are exceptions, however, such as hippos. Those are harvested with headshots, and as long as the shot damages the brain, your Hunt Rating won't go down.

When you place a good shot, you'll notice a significant splash of blood at the location where the animal was shot. Analyze it to see how successful you were. The analysis will help you find out whether the animal will survive or not.

In many cases, the animal won't die on the spot. If you had Ammunition of the correct Tier and shot with enough Energy, indicated by Hunter assist as you shoot, it means that you may not have damaged vital organs enough or at all, and you'll have to track it down.

Ask your dog companion to do this, or solve this riddle by yourself. It's easier to follow the trail when the initial blood splash is larger. The meat of dead animals will degrade, so the faster you claim your harvest, the more you earn.

When you claim your harvest, you'll see a highly detailed overview of your shot, as well as the harvest quality. The overview displays both the amount of damage dealt to each organ (the higher, the better) and the amount of meat lost (the higher, the worse). Don't confuse them! Finally, you can make the call and decide whether you want to sell or taxidermy it.
The higher their Fitness, the larger Trophies animals have. So it's worth investing in wildlife management, habitat recovery and enhancement!

Culling means selectively harvesting animals with undesirable characteristics. Animals are culled based on their Fitness, sex, and age. Target younger animals with low Fitness and preferably male. You can also cull female animals, especially the young ones with low Fitness, but it'll have a slightly smaller effect on the population.

One year of animal life equals 3 in-game days. Once animals reach the final year of their life span, they disappear, and new animals appear instead. So the final year is when you harvest to get the best Trophy and the least negative impact on the Population.

Note that culling only applies to the Land where the harvested animal lived. Animals of the same Species from other Lands won't be affected. So if you manage Moose from Thunderbird Muskeg, it only affects other Moose from the same area.
When Populations are Vulnerable, you won't see animals with high Fitness in them. Stable Populations are average, while Healthy and Thriving ones reliably produce animals with the best Trophies.

To cull the right animals, observe which animals in groups have the lowest Fitness. They're your targets! For species that lead mostly solitary lives, such as Moose, you'll have to scout the whole Land and see which Moose have the lowest Fitness.

Improving Populations from Vulnerable to Stable and from Stable to Healthy is slow. Don't worry if you don't see an immediate result. As long as you target the lowest-Fitness animals within the borders of the Land where you hunt, you'll eventually start seeing animals with higher Fitness!

No matter how large a Trophy is, you can’t call it ultimate if it's just like any other trophy but bigger. The most sought-after Trophies are the ones that are both large and belong to animals with one of the rarer conditions.

Rare conditions include albinism (white fur, red eyes), leucism (white fur, standard eyes), melanism (black or dark fur) and erythrism (pink or reddish fur). You'll have to get lucky to bag one of these with a huge Trophy!

Always be on the lookout for these ultimate Trophies and taxidermy them. They're valuable, sure, but this is how you build a collection that will be the envy of any visiting hunter, a collection to be proud of.

Check all past harvests in your Hunting log. This is where you learn what kind of Trophies each level of animal Fitness brings. Remember that it's always a question of probability. Nothing is certain in nature, except eventual death!
Smart animals conceal themselves in high cover. To force them out, hunters use callers, decoys, and lures.
Callers imitate animal vocalizations such as mating, warning and territorial calls. Use them when you want to expose a nearby animal or when there isn't much cover, so stalking would expose you.
Get downwind of the animals so they can't catch your scent. Then start calling, but only produce calls sporadically. You can check the optimal timing for each caller in the Encyclopedia.
Once the animal's curiosity is piqued and it starts to approach slowly, it's on the hook. Just don't start spamming calls, or the animal may find them unnatural and may even be spooked.

Decoys create visual anchors for animals. The more you set them up in the area, the more they are likely to work. Place decoys near lakeshores where waterfowls often congregate or in open fields that would force landfowl to expose themselves.

Make sure you're not too far away from the decoys once you place them. Call your target with a caller so that it can notice the decoy. Remember that decoys will drop down to the ground in time, so you have to go back and manually set them up to use them again.

Lures contain scents that animals find irresistible. These scents are less reliable than decoys because they are carried by the wind and fade quickly. So either use them on animals that are passing by closely or only after you call the target to the place where you expect the wind to carry the scent.

It is not just about harvesting animals. It is about ensuring that you harvest them in the best state. What it usually means is you should make the animal drop as fast as possible while making sure as little damage as possible is done.

Animals are organized into Tiers. Tiers are numbers that communicate how much energy your shots require to get to vital organs. The heavier the animal, the higher the Tier and the more powerful ammunition you need. You can check the Tier of each species and ammunition in the Encyclopedia.
Just getting the right Tier is never enough. You should also make sure that you use the appropriate ammunition at the right distance.

How can you tell the difference? This is where Hunter assist comes in. When you are aiming for a shot, you will see a visual indication whether the expected energy you will produce is appropriate for the animal. If you’re too close, you may damage the animal too much, so move away, and vice versa.

Ethical harvests are effective harvests. The less time the animal suffers, the better meat you get, the better your hunt score. This is why it is always crucial to aim to the vital organs, the heart and both lungs, and ignore everything else.

You can tell how effective your shot was not only by the time the animal stays alive, but by the amount of blood and blood colors. Lots of red or bright pink blood with bubbles indicates a successful lung shot, meaning you did a good job.
Smaller amounts of dark red blood, brownish hues and processed food fragments indicate that you should go to the Shooting range and work on your aiming.

The American foxhound is primarily a blood-tracking breed that can also look for older animal Tracks. With time and repetition, foxhounds will follow your commands reliably (increased obedience), heel, sit and stay for longer, remain closer and behave calmer when released. Accomplish it all by bonding and improving their aptitudes.

Dogs don't alert animals with the noises they make, they can only spook game by getting very close. So bring them on hunts to gradually bond and give them commands to bond even more. When commands are followed properly, pet the dog so the corresponding aptitude improves faster. Don't take too long, or the foxhound won't link the behavior with your reward.

Your companion has focus shown. The higher it is, the more the aptitude for any successful command grows, so when the focus is low, the dog receives less experience. Focus gradually recovers as long as you aren't giving new commands. You can also send the dog home for faster recovery, but the bond won't be growing during this time.

When foxhounds quarter, they zigzag back and forth to search for blood and other Tracks. This way, they can also find shot-down birds and dead small game in tall grass, but only if they're very close. When your dog finds the initial hit blood and the next part of the Track is too far, you may need to explicitly command to track blood further. The better the aptitude for this is, the longer foxhounds stay on the Track. Your companion will also wait for you if it gets too far ahead!

blocks.p: Pick a weapon in three steps: it must cover the animal's tier, then the lower its accuracy number the better, then lower recoil and noise are a bonus.

list: Tiers: the animal tiers this weapon's ammunition is rated for. The animal's tier (on its page) must be in this range.
Accuracy: how far a shot can stray from where you aim. Lower is better: excellent 0.65 or less, good up to 1.05, fair up to 2.2, wide above that (shotguns, bows).
Recoil: how hard it kicks. Lower keeps the animal in the scope for a second shot.
Noise: how far animals hear the shot (game units). Lower spooks fewer animals. '-' = the game gives no noise value.
Sway is the same for every weapon: it comes from your stance, breathing, bipods and shooting sticks.

blocks.p: With hunter assist on, the circle shows where your shot can land at the distance you aim at. Its size comes from the weapon's accuracy plus your own skill plus the load's accuracy: a 2 MOA rifle at 200 m draws a circle about 23 cm across on the animal, so a more accurate rifle really does draw a smaller circle. Green = a good hit on the animal, red = not a good hit, beige = it lands on terrain. Shotgun shot shows no circle.
The assist follows the live wind: the impact point it shows moves with the wind as soon as it blows, without waiting for a first shot.

blocks.p: You get skill points as you level up. Spend them on skills in the five trees (Hunter > Skills in the game). Each tree is a pyramid: one skill at the top, more below it, and the lower skills cost more.

list: Levels 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21: 1 point each

blocks.note: You can't have every skill: 23 points against 98. The game lets you reset your skills and spend the points again.

Juniper's been training dogs since she was a child. She has trained dogs for agility and self-defense, but now she considers hunting the ultimate challenge because she likes to put the dog to the test in a category they were bred for.

facts: Skittish, introverted, prefers the company of dogs rather than people
Best dog trainer in the United States, dog whisperer?

list: Juniper and her dog, Bug, both have heterochromia, which means that they have different-colored eyes.
Juniper suffers from sleep paralysis, but it's improving thanks to Bug. She's been training her as a service dog to monitor her condition.

blocks.p:
Patrick is a warden of New Laurentia, always looking for ways to promote the reserve. You'll often see him in pink glasses, a furry coat, and with a well-groomed, stylish beard.

Recently, he went through what his wife jokingly calls an "end-life crisis." He started buying high-end gadgets for fun and completely overhauled his wardrobe. Now he brightens up every space he enters with his personality. He doesn’t shy away from being the center of attention and somehow manages to even sound louder.

facts: Courageous, extroverted. Prefers to hunt for attention in packs.

list: Patrick became best friends with Malachi Burnett on the Hearth & Hunt forum, without ever meeting in person! They bonded over meat aging techniques.
Patrick fell in love with his wife Regina after she predicted his death and then saved him.

blocks.p:
Often called "the beating heart of New Laurentia," and it still doesn't do her justice. She's in charge of habitat enhancement and animal welfare in the reserve, though her methods are anything but conventional. 
Regina relies heavily on her intuition, dreams and a deep sense of spirituality.

She believes that nature is the most powerful force in the world and that humans should serve it instead of trying to control it. Lately, however, a quiet melancholy has taken hold of her. She feels her husband is growing more distant and she can’t understand why. To cope, she throws herself even deeper into her work—which is great for us!

facts: Leader of the pack, courageous, prefers to live in the forest

list: Organizes annual pageants Miss New Laurentia, starring the "prettiest" animals from the reserve. Somehow, moose always end up winning... Rumor has it it's rigged.
Regina published her own cookbook named "Make It From Scratch! + Edible Flowers Collection." The cookbook became a hit thanks to its cocktail recipes.

blocks.p: Angel is a rep for several reserves in the Pacific Northwest. He's been doing this for 12 years now. He is also the second-oldest son in the Hearth family and the fourth in the Hearth & Hunt family.

facts: Probably hates his job, but WHY won't he quit?
Hates his family, but himself even MORE, LOSER

list: I KNOW WHERE HE LIVES (contact me if you want to know too)
HE IS NOT YOUR FRIEND

blocks.p:
Malachi used to be a safari guide for the ultra-wealthy, but over time, he grew tired of human companions. These days, he often jokes that he's developed a touch of misanthropy, and if he can handle everything via email or from afar, that’s exactly how he prefers it. He’s now the co-owner of the tourist business Panorama Inc. alongside his friend, Sydney.

Malachi enjoys sitting in front of his laptop with a good cup of coffee. While others might tease him about wanting to return to the thrill of the hunt, he has no such desire. He feels older than he really is and simply craves peace and quiet. He is a great asset for Hearth & Hunt and we are glad to have him on board.

list: Have you heard about Malachi's daughter Hailey? No? That's impossible, he talks about her all the time.
Malachi once made a fan page for Hailey. He only deleted it because she discovered it and was scared that she had a stalker.
Malachi plans to visit Patrick for the first time in New Laurentia this year for his birthday. He already bought gifts, a professional lighting setup and a selfie stick!

blocks.p:
Damian is a trickster shooter and a self-proclaimed master of the bow, possibly the best, if you ask him. He’s loud, a bit narcissistic, and flat-out refuses to admit failure, so dealing with him may be a bit difficult.

We hired him to deliver a lecture on advanced bow shooting for our clients. But there was a catch: Damian isn’t exactly teacher material. His thoughts tend to scatter, he bounces from topic to topic with wild energy. He only manages to channel it when he’s got a bow in his hands and a target in sight.

facts: Loud, may alert animals in the vicinity
The best bow shooter you can find

list: Damian has surprisingly good wood-crafting skills and sometimes makes wooden figures for his friends. But he hides this skill because he doesn’t consider it "cool" enough.
Damian has never played a video game in his life.

blocks.p:
Naomi used to be a part of Hearth & Hunt, but she recently left us for undisclosed reasons. She's a wonderful hunter with skills and experience like no one else, so we need to get her back.

Naomi grew up in Kilimaya Reserve. She used to hunt with her father and his business clients. Her father owns a tea brand and grows most of his products in Kilimaya. They travelled across the globe and joined Hearth & Hunt when she was a child.

Naomi is sharp-minded and well-educated. She gravitates toward intellectuals, especially her closest friend Pandora Hearth.

list: Naomi never drinks alcohol, always preferring a fresh cup of tea. She has quite the expertise, so if you’re offered some—always take it.
Naomi owns 5 dogs, 2 cats, 2 tortoises, 25 chickens and 1 parrot.

blocks.p: The only adopted child of Genevieve Hearth. The rumor is that she was given Kilimaya Reserve as some sort of sick joke. But it was Pandora who asked specifically to be in charge of Kilimaya Reserve, even though her mother didn't allow it at first because of Pandora's skin condition. She may seem like an airhead, but she is standing firmly on the ground, always with a plan.

facts: Hearth & Hunt coordinator in charge of Kilimaya Reserve
Stealthy, she may stand behind you and you wouldn't know about it
She is a morning person who had to switch to night shifts due to her skin condition.
Albinism, has to cover up her skin non-stop due to the climate in Kilimaya Reserve

list: Pandora is a staring competition winner who remains unchallenged.
Pandora is the second youngest child in the Hearth & Hunt family.

blocks.p: Hearth & Hunt's carpenter and builder, waiting for you at the Hearth & Hunt Headquarters. He builds the lodge expansions, and he knows a thing or two more: mushrooms, and people - "those two aren't that different".

facts: Carpenter and builder for Hearth & Hunt
Being on his own - and Mikael Anderson

list: He is Irish, and says that once the Irish thought more of fairies than of food when they saw a mushroom.
He got a world-record hunter's signature in Kilimaya Reserve and cooked him amakhowe mushrooms, a local delicacy.
He swears by Regina Harper's dreams - he ignored one once and calls it the biggest mistake of his life.
Talk to him about people: it is his favourite subject.

blocks.p: Hearth & Hunt's former representative in New Laurentia - the hunter you are replacing. He comes from Lintukoto Reserve, speaks plainly, and has looked after an elk herd for years. He shows you how animal daily routines work.

facts: Former Hearth & Hunt representative in New Laurentia
Fox fires, Loudest deer, Pack dynamics, One shot, no waste

blocks.p: Juniper's dog, a blood-tracking dog she is training for a national competition. She shows up in Juniper's missions in New Laurentia - including the night she goes missing.
